props.title: Ronin
props.initialSlug: Mercenaries chase a mysterious briefcase across France

sections.content: Ronin (1998) stands as one of the last great practical-effects action thrillers before CGI dominated Hollywood. Director John Frankenheimer, who revolutionized car chases in The French Connection (1971), delivers jaw-dropping Paris and Nice pursuits that influenced everything from The Bourne Identity (2002) to Mission: Impossible - Fallout (2018). Robert De Niro leads a crew of masterless operatives (like their samurai namesakes) in a labyrinthine plot involving a mysterious briefcase - a MacGuffin that echoes Pulp Fiction (1994) while focusing on the paranoid professionalism of its post-Cold War mercenaries.

sections.content: The film's European setting and emphasis on tradecraft links it to classic 70s espionage like The Day of the Jackal (1973) and Three Days of the Condor (1975). Frankenheimer's direction emphasizes realism - real cars, real crashes, real locations - creating a tangible tension missing from modern green-screen spectacles. The international cast including Jean Reno and Stellan Skarsgård adds authentic European flavor while avoiding Hollywood clichés.

What sets Ronin apart is its commitment to showing professional criminals as true professionals. Like Thief (1981) or The Driver (1978), it's obsessed with the technical details of its world. Characters discuss makes of guns and cars with casual expertise. The famous ambush scene demonstrates tactical awareness that influenced later films like Sicario (2015) and Den of Thieves (2018). sections.content: Ronin's car chases deserve special attention as masterclasses in practical stunt work and editing. Using over 300 stunt drivers, Frankenheimer shoots the pursuits with a ground-level immediacy that makes modern CGI chases feel weightless in comparison. The influence is clear in films like Baby Driver (2017) and Drive (2011), which similarly emphasize practical effects and driver skill over digital enhancement.
